title: Reflections from the Women and Girls' Online Safety Conference 2025
hook: My personal highlights and takeaways from a conference on Building a Shared Understanding of Online Harms, organised by the Centre for Protecting Women Online at the Open University, UK.

body.text: Did you know that 99% of deepfake images online are of women and girls? Technology continues to become more pervasive in our lives, creating yet another channel and site of violence against women and girls.

As someone professionally working in violence prevention and personally cautious of the manipulation of attention economy that feeds tech platforms, I hoped this space would help me become more aware and provide direction for action to make the online world safer and kinder. The two-day inaugural conference exceeded my expectations in both breadth and depth.
Five takeaways on tech-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV)
Tech-facilitated gender-based violence encompasses the use of digital technologies to perpetrate, facilitate, or amplify violence against women and girls.

Below I synthesize five key themes that emerged for me personally, across multiple presentations and panels I attended throughout the conference, drawing on insights from researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and advocates working in this field.
1. A “new face to an old problem” with commonalities and uniqueness

Most cases of intimate partner violence now have some kind of cyber element attached to them. TFGBV cuts across not only online and offline spheres but also national borders. It uses the same tactics of isolation, intimidation, victim-blaming and silencing of women as offline violence. What’s unique about TFGBV is its scale, reach and lack of accountability and consequences for both perpetrators and platforms.
Just like offline GBV, it is vast in its scope. Some examples of GBV or underlying factors that stood out to me:

items.label: Surveillance as “care”:
items.text: Smart devices are being used to monitor partners under the guise of protection and love.

items.label: Online strategizing of abuse:
items.text: Anonymous online forums serve as spaces where some users post about GBV perpetration (as well as help-seeking) strategies while many more consume this information. Anonymous commenters sometimes encourage others to escalate the violence, suggesting lack of proper moderation.

items.label: Deepfakes targeting women:
items.text: A staggering 99% of deepfake images online are of women and girls. Several harmful myths perpetuate this abuse, such as justifying deepfakes by equating them to “using one’s imagination”.

items.label: Bias in artificial intelligence systems:
items.text: Research uncovered gender and Global North bias embedded in AI chatbots that are increasingly used across the world. These biases can work in covert ways making them harder to test explicitly.

items.label: Silencing through harassment:
items.text: Online trolling and unsafe digital spaces cause women, including activists, to withdraw from important political conversations.

items.label: Rising and profitable anti-feminist narratives:
items.text: What was especially concerning is the profitability of the seemingly rising “manfluencer strategy”. These content creators target young boys and men on platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and podcasts with anti-women narratives and regressive gender norms, creating a sense of belonging to a community. The insidious business model needs attention: the more controversial or shocking the content, the greater the potential for algorithms to make it go viral, generating more views and eventually more profits for creators.

body.text: A slide from the presentation “The Online Radicalization of Young Boys in the Manosphere: A Rising Threat to Women’s Online Safety” by Lavinia Rotundi, illustrating how algorithms funnel young men toward increasingly misogynistic content.
2. The need to keep up with changes in communications and culture

There seem to be significant normative shifts at play that need to be better understood and strategically responded to. For instance, using technology for surveillance as care and “protection” (by parents or lovers) may be impacting how young people understand the idea of love. The spread of harmful gender norms that perpetuate or justify violence against women and girls, and understanding who profits from it requires attention. Additionally, while technology is progressing rapidly, digital literacy and legislation are not keeping pace.

There is a need for those working in violence prevention to study and understand these broader cultural shifts and tailor their programs to speak to the current context. For example, the 112 Iceland app makes it possible to contact 112 during emergencies without calling. The speaker shared that the app works better for violence reporting because youth no longer like talking on the phone. Similarly, “Equally Safe Online” programme researchers who train AI bots to address harmful online content emphasized the importance of working in close collaboration with young people who understood the nuances of phrases and language signifying online abuse, as well as appropriate responses that wouldn’t be considered “cringe”.
3. Asking where is the political will and who holds the power?

During the discussion, it was repeatedly acknowledged by different speakers that a power imbalance exists between political states and technology companies, whose reach is global. With limited regulation and TFGBV being a cross-border issue, governments largely rely on tech companies’ self-regulation, an approach that has proven inadequate and conflicts with their profit motives. We don’t have safety by design.

There appears to be low political will or even public demand to address this issue, reasons for which need to be further unpacked. It is important to understand this and consider what is needed to embolden political and public pressure to bring about better regulation to prevent TFGBV. We have seen examples, especially around child safeguarding, where advocacy has helped, and we need to think about what lessons can be drawn from such precedents.
4. So what are the solutions?

To address TFGBV, speakers said we need a broad approach that requires collaboration among a range of groups with diverse expertise and focus areas. There is no single solution. Several ongoing efforts were highlighted:

items.label: Prevention and education:
items.text: School-based programs promoting gender equality alongside digital awareness and literacy on online harms.

items.label: Harnessing AI for good:
items.text: Exploring positive uses of AI to combat online violence, including training AI systems to detect and predict harms and to respond effectively. A speaker mentioned the idea of envisioning feminist AI, reimagining AI systems built on equity, kindness and care.

items.label: Maintaining a broad perspective:
items.text: Cross-sector collaboration and working with different stakeholders, from legislators and law enforcement to online platforms and tech companies, is critical.

items.label: Ethical technology design:
items.text: Moving beyond reactive responses to address how technology is designed in the first place, embedding values such as kindness and safety right from design.

body.text: This discussion left me reflecting on the power of feminist movements to counter anti-feminist narratives. What kind of online content might be needed to shift harmful gender norms at the scale and speed that technology operates?
5. The power of storytelling and reclaiming the narrative

A huge shout out to filmmaker Patricia Franquesa, who shared her powerful, acclaimed documentary (My Sextortion Diary) about her real life experience of online sextortion. It was palpable and deeply moving, highlighting the impact of humanizing such experiences of violence. Her film illustrated not only the harassment she faced and the lack of understanding and support from official duty-bearers (to no avail or consequence), but also how she ultimately chose to reclaim her narrative and power. Her courageous work is a gift and service to the world, and we need to take note.

In the Q&A, she shared something striking: her faceless abusers could share her private photos without accountability, yet when she sought to share them herself, she was forced to censor them. This raises a critical question: who is really being empowered by technology, and where does accountability lie?

Post-screening discussion of Patricia Franquesa’s documentary “My Sextortion Diary”. The discussion became a space for processing collective grief, anger, and hope that the documentary evoked among the audience.
Final reflections

I appreciated the thoughtful planning that went into creating a friendly environment (much needed especially when discussing such difficult topics) and the effort taken to make space for a range of perspectives — research, practice, policy, survivor experiences — through impressive and engaging presentations, panels and an excellent documentary. This was just their first conference, so I am sure there are many more good offerings in store for the future. A big thanks to the Gender Violence Early Career Network for supporting my participation.

I came out of the space feeling a mix of emotions. On the one hand, I felt cynical about the state of the world — the scale and various manifestations of TFGBV, the power imbalances, the profit motives that disregard harm. On the other hand, I was deeply grateful to see many committed people come together to have honest conversations, exchange learning, discuss ideas and solutions and reflect on who else needs to be part of this conversation.

The work ahead is clearer: we need stronger regulation and accountability in technology, better digital literacy, ethical technology design, and powerful counter-narratives. But perhaps most importantly, we need to keep having these conversations — in academic spaces, policy circles, tech companies, and with our friends and family. The online world doesn’t have to replicate and amplify offline violence. We need to come together and demand something better.
If you’re interested in learning more about this work, I encourage you to follow the Centre for Protecting Women Online and explore Patricia Franquesa’s documentary, My Sextortion Diary.

title: Pausing and reflecting in a moment of professional transition
hook: Three lessons from five years at a feminist activist organisation in Uganda — on the personal in the professional, process over output, and solidarity over competition.

body.text: In 2020, at the start of the pandemic, I made a professional shift. I moved from a large international research organization to a small (but mighty!) Uganda-based activist and feminist organization. I joined Raising Voices to be more grounded in real world challenges, learn about violence prevention and contribute through my research skills. In my early years of joining, I recall noting with awe how the organization was strategy and values driven, and the role-modelling and encouragement to bring our whole selves to work. Over time, I became the Learning Coordinator, getting the opportunity to lead the learning work and becoming more involved in issues related to organizational and team management. This role expanded my researcher identity to a researcher-practitioner-activist identity wherein I got to understand and relate to practitioner perspectives and priorities.

I have now moved on from this position and have relocated from Uganda, a place I have been lucky to call home since 2018. The past few months of transition have been overwhelming. Finally the dust is settling, and I want to take this moment to acknowledge three lessons learnt that have shaped my view of the world, lessons that I want to carry forward with me. The insights I share are drawn from my own personal experience and may not be reflective of others’ experiences or perspectives.
Embracing the personal (and emotional) in ‘professional’ while also appreciating and upholding boundaries

Violence prevention work, including research on violence, is personal work that impacts how we engage with the world. While I subconsciously knew this, working at Raising Voices brought that to the fore even more for me, nudging me to integrate my personal and professional life more meaningfully. I found unsaid permission to be emotional and express myself. I saw joy be cultivated intentionally, while also holding space for anxiety and grief. I appreciated an informal organizational culture including encouragement to prioritize time for self-care. I saw how trust is built when people came together to support one another during personal hardships. In thoughtfully curated retreats, we prioritized connection and reflection, sharing stories from our lives and celebrating one another. It is in this environment I decided to write and share about my own experiences that drew me to violence prevention work, connect those to broader activism and feel a sense of compassion, dignity and solidarity from others that fuels and sustains my work. The journey’s been a bit like joining post-work Zumba sessions or team ice-breakers. At first, I was embarrassed and at times mortified, but once I started feeling safer and comfortable, I had a great time being me in front of my co-workers!

While I have happily embraced how personal our work is, it is not to be confused with not having personal boundaries at work which are important to both set and respect, perhaps especially so in the non-profit sector where one’s vulnerabilities and passion is at risk of exploitation. I also continue to learn to not take things personally. To hold space for and appreciate different opinions and perspectives. I think it’s a lesson we all probably learn again and again in our lives? To let go, or perhaps to choose wisely what to not let go.
The practice of emphasizing ‘process over output’ for more rigorous values-driven work

Working in a feminist organization that frequently and collectively reflects on its identity and values, and what it translates to in day-to-day practice, showed me the value of focusing on the process of our work, be it programming, learning, partnerships or creating a vibrant organizational and team culture. Rigor and quality comes from paying attention to the overall process, rather than focusing solely on outputs. This often requires working collectively, which can be slower than working individually, but if done with intention the impact and quality is far greater and more sustainable. At Raising Voices, I experienced this practice in action: in routine collective participatory processes which brought together all staff in a circle to ask critical questions and contribute to organization-wide strategy and direction; in everyday relationship-building with co-workers and collaborators that went beyond the surface; in acknowledging difficult moments and addressing challenges; in a process of iterative learning that celebrates successes and learns from challenges and is concerned with integrating knowledge and converting it into action.

Particularly in my role, I came to appreciate the power of practice-based learning and the urgent need to value, nurture and elevate it, and got several opportunities to share and discuss this thinking with diverse actors in the violence prevention field.

A brainstorming discussion during a Learning Team retreat. I really enjoyed our annual learning team retreats — it is a space where I felt deeply connected to the work, engaged in deep strategic collective thinking, and also laughed and cried!
Nurturing a voice of boldness and solidarity

One of Raising Voices’ organizational values is “spirited activism”. When I first joined I felt disconnected with this value. I saw myself as a feminist but not really an activist. I was in the research and evaluation field and I felt boxed in an identity that I took to mean objectivity and a lack of passion. So over the years, reflecting on ‘spirited activism’ helped me connect with my internal motivations of pursuing this work as well as challenge how I see and understand research. I learnt that there are different ways of being an activist that feels aligned with one’s personality, and that activism is a muscle that can be strengthened over time through small acts. And as a researcher, one can be an activist too — in fact, research and learning isn’t values neutral and can be feminist. Along with the Learning team, I expanded my understanding of feminist principles of learning and what it means to apply them in practice.
The vibrant Raising Voices & CEDOVIP values mural you’ll find displayed on the office walls.

I also learnt what solidarity looks like and how much we need it. I recall initially perceiving that all different methodologies for violence prevention are competing with each other for funding and in demonstration of their impact. That thinking has evolved over time, whereby I now better appreciate the need and contribution of different interventions, while also acknowledging the broader funding context that drives competition. Shifting from the competition mindset to one of solidarity has helped me see others working in this field from a point of appreciation, curiosity and learning. I have been inspired by witnessing the fruits of collective advocacy and collaboration. At the same time, solidarity has meant supporting “elevation” of that which is “closest to injustice” and seeking accountability for the women and children our work intends to be in service of. Language matters too — seeing communities as partners rather than ‘field’ and ‘beneficiaries’ can be a small step to changing one’s orientation towards this work.

I am immensely grateful to Raising Voices, and to all the people who make it what it is. I continue to support a few learning initiatives at Raising Voices in a different capacity. I am now based in London, UK.
